figures.title: The Bioactives Family Tree
figures.subtitle: Plant compounds that are not essential nutrients, in four families.

segments.name: Bioactives
segments.text: This lesson is about bioactives: compounds in food that aren't essential nutrients, so there's no deficiency disease, but that still act on the body. Most come from plants, which make them as pigments, defenses or signals.

segments.name: Polyphenols and Terpenoids
segments.text: The tree sorts them into four chemical families. Polyphenols, built on rings with OH groups, include flavonoids and other phenols. Terpenoids, built from five-carbon isoprene units, include carotenoids and phytosterols.

segments.name: Sulfur, Spice and Stimulants
segments.text: Sulfur compounds like sulforaphane and allicin give the cabbage and onion families their bite. And the spice and stimulant compounds, capsaicin and caffeine, act on nerve receptors.

segments.name: Foods
segments.text: The bottom row shows the foods richest in each. Each box links to its figure.

segments.name: Whole Foods First
segments.text: Diets rich in fruit, vegetables, tea, coffee, whole grains and legumes are consistently linked to better health. But isolated bioactives in pills mostly haven't matched those results, and a few have backfired.

figures.title: Flavonoids
figures.subtitle: What a phenol is, and three flavonoids: quercetin, anthocyanins and isoflavones.

segments.name: Phenol
segments.text: Start with phenol: an OH group on a benzene ring. A polyphenol has several. That OH easily gives up its hydrogen to quench a reactive molecule, which makes polyphenols antioxidants in a test tube.

segments.name: Quercetin
segments.text: Flavonoids are the largest polyphenol group, and they all share one fifteen-carbon skeleton: two rings joined through a middle ring with an oxygen. Quercetin is the most common flavonol, in onions, kale, apples, berries and tea.

segments.name: What Flavonoids Do
segments.text: Little is absorbed intact; the liver and gut bacteria change most of it, and the products may calm inflammation and help blood vessels relax. Diets high in flavonoid-rich foods are linked to lower heart disease and stroke risk.

segments.name: Anthocyanins
segments.text: In anthocyanins, like cyanidin, the middle oxygen carries a positive charge and the molecule becomes a pigment: the red, purple and blue of berries and red cabbage. The color shifts with acidity, so red cabbage turns blue with baking soda.

segments.name: Isoflavones
segments.text: In isoflavones like genistein, the second ring sits one carbon over, so it weakly fits estrogen receptors. They come mainly from soy, and normal intake of soy foods is considered safe.

figures.title: Other Polyphenols
figures.subtitle: Resveratrol, chlorogenic acid in coffee, and hydroxytyrosol in olive oil.

segments.name: Resveratrol
segments.text: Resveratrol is two phenol rings joined by a double bond, made by grapes to fight fungus. It extended lifespan in some animals, but human trials have disappointed, and a glass of red wine has only a tiny amount.

segments.name: Chlorogenic Acid
segments.text: Chlorogenic acid is quinic acid joined through an ester to caffeic acid, the phenol part. It's the main polyphenol in coffee, adding bitterness and acidity.

segments.name: Coffee
segments.text: For many adults coffee is the biggest source of polyphenols, and moderate coffee drinking is linked to lower risk of type 2 diabetes and liver disease. Roasting breaks chlorogenic acid down, so light roasts keep more.

segments.name: Hydroxytyrosol
segments.text: Hydroxytyrosol has the same pair of neighboring OH groups as quercetin and caffeic acid. It's the main polyphenol of extra-virgin olive oil and part of its peppery bite.

segments.name: Olive Oil
segments.text: The EU allows a claim that olive oil polyphenols help protect blood lipids from oxidation, for oils with enough of them. Refining removes most, which is one reason extra-virgin oil is thought to do more.

figures.title: Carotenoids
figures.subtitle: Isoprene chains that color food orange and red.

segments.name: Isoprene
segments.text: Terpenoids are built from isoprene, a five-carbon unit with one branch. Eight of them make a carotenoid.

segments.name: Beta-Carotene
segments.text: Beta-carotene has a ring at each end joined by a long chain of alternating double bonds. That chain absorbs blue light, so it looks orange. Cut in the middle, it makes two molecules of vitamin A.

segments.name: Too Much
segments.text: Your gut only converts what you need, so food beta-carotene can't cause vitamin A poisoning; a lot just tints the skin orange, harmlessly. But high-dose supplements raised lung cancer risk in smokers, so smokers should avoid them.

segments.name: Lycopene
segments.text: Lycopene has the same formula but open ends, and its fully flat chain makes it red. It's the color of tomatoes and watermelon and isn't turned into vitamin A. Cooking with a little fat makes it far more available, so tomato sauce beats raw tomatoes.

segments.name: Lutein
segments.text: Two more: lutein and zeaxanthin collect in the eye's macula and filter blue light. Kale, spinach, corn and egg yolk are good sources.

figures.title: Phytosterols
figures.subtitle: The plant twin of cholesterol, which blocks its absorption.

segments.name: Two Sterols
segments.text: Here's cholesterol from the Lipids lesson: four fused rings, an OH and a carbon tail. Next to it is beta-sitosterol, the main plant sterol, which is the same molecule with two extra carbons on the tail.

segments.name: Crowding Out
segments.text: Because they look so alike, plant sterols crowd cholesterol out of the bile mixtures that carry it into gut cells. Less cholesterol is absorbed, both from food and from what your liver sends into the gut.

segments.name: How Much
segments.text: About two grams a day lowers LDL cholesterol by roughly eight to ten percent within a few weeks, and the FDA and EU allow heart-health claims for foods with added sterols or stanols.

segments.name: Found In
segments.text: They're in vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, wheat germ and legumes, but a normal diet gives only a fraction of a gram, so reaching two grams takes fortified spreads, yogurts or drinks.

segments.name: Who Should Avoid
segments.text: Very little is absorbed. People with the rare disorder sitosterolemia do absorb them and should avoid them.

figures.title: Sulforaphane and Allicin
figures.subtitle: The sulfur compounds of broccoli and garlic, made when you cut them.

segments.name: Glucoraphanin
segments.text: Broccoli stores glucoraphanin, a glucosinolate: a sulfur chain parked on a glucose. When you cut or chew it, the enzyme myrosinase cuts the glucose off, and the rest rearranges into sulforaphane, with an N=C=S group.

segments.name: What It Does
segments.text: Sulforaphane switches on Nrf2, a signal that raises the body's own detoxifying and antioxidant enzymes. Brassica-rich diets are linked to lower risk of some cancers; trials of sulforaphane itself are early.

segments.name: Getting the Most
segments.text: To get the most, chop or chew it raw or lightly steamed. Hard boiling destroys myrosinase, but a pinch of mustard powder on cooked broccoli adds it back. Broccoli sprouts have by far the most.

segments.name: Allicin
segments.text: Garlic works the same way. Crushing it lets the enzyme alliinase make allicin, two sulfurs side by side. It soon breaks down into the sulfur compounds that carry garlic's smell.

segments.name: Garlic Evidence
segments.text: Garlic's sulfur compounds kill microbes in the lab and may slightly lower blood pressure and cholesterol, though the evidence is modest. Onions, leeks and chives make related compounds, including the one that makes you cry.

figures.title: Capsaicin and Other Pungent Compounds
figures.subtitle: Chili, black pepper and ginger, and why they feel hot.

segments.name: Capsaicin
segments.text: Capsaicin has a vanilla-like ring head, an amide link and a fatty tail. That tail is why it dissolves in fat and milk, not water.

segments.name: Why It Burns
segments.text: Capsaicin switches on TRPV1, the nerve receptor for dangerous heat, so your mouth feels burning with no real burn. With repeated exposure the nerves become less sensitive, which is why capsaicin creams are used for pain.

segments.name: Cooling Down
segments.text: Very hot peppers can cause pain and vomiting. Milk and fatty foods cool the burn better than water. Most of the heat is in the white ribs, not the seeds.

segments.name: Piperine
segments.text: Black pepper's piperine also has an amide and also triggers heat receptors, more mildly. It slows the breakdown of some compounds, which is why it's paired with turmeric.

segments.name: Gingerol
segments.text: Ginger's gingerol has capsaicin's head with a ketone and OH in its chain; drying or cooking turns it into the even sharper shogaol. Ginger modestly eases nausea in several trials.

figures.title: Caffeine and Theobromine
figures.subtitle: The stimulants of coffee, tea and chocolate.

segments.name: Caffeine
segments.text: Caffeine is a purine, related to the A and G of DNA, with three methyl groups. Theobromine, from cocoa, has an N-H in place of one.

segments.name: How It Works
segments.text: Caffeine blocks adenosine, the brain signal that builds up sleepiness. It takes effect in fifteen to forty-five minutes and lasts, with a half-life of about five hours.

segments.name: How Much Is Safe
segments.text: The FDA says up to 400 milligrams a day generally isn't linked to harm in healthy adults; in pregnancy the guidance is 200 or less. Too much brings jitters, a racing heart and poor sleep. And theobromine is toxic to dogs.

segments.name: Caffeine Amounts
segments.text: A cup of brewed coffee has about 80 to 100 milligrams, black tea about half that, cola about 30 to 40, and an ounce of dark chocolate 12 to 25.

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: The whole lesson in one table, plus a few extras.

segments.name: One Table
segments.text: Here's the whole lesson in one table: each bioactive, its family, what it may do, where it's found, and what's good to know.

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras. Test-tube antioxidant scores don't predict effects in the body. Grapefruit contains bioactives that raise the blood levels of many medicines. And some compounds, like tannins and glucosinolates, are antinutrients or bioactives depending on the dose and the diet.
